{{Short description|Smooth 4-manifold homeomorphic yet not diffeomorphic to Euclidean space}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Exotic '''R'''<sup>4</sup>}}
{{technical|date=May 2021}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''exotic''' <math>\R^4</math> is a [[differentiable manifold]] that is [[homeomorphic]] (i.e. shape preserving) but not [[diffeomorphism|diffeomorphic]] (i.e. non smooth) to the [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^4.</math> The first examples were found in 1982 by [[Michael Freedman]] and others, by using the contrast between Freedman's theorems about topological 4-manifolds, and [[Simon Donaldson]]'s theorems about smooth 4-manifolds.<ref>Kirby (1989), p. 95</ref><ref>Freedman and Quinn (1990), p. 122</ref> There is a [[cardinality of the continuum|continuum]] of non-diffeomorphic [[differentiable structure]]s <math>\R^4,</math> as was shown first by [[Clifford Taubes]].<ref>Taubes (1987), Theorem 1.1</ref>

Prior to this construction, non-diffeomorphic [[smooth structure]]s on spheres{{snd}}[[exotic sphere]]s{{snd}}were already known to exist, although the question of the existence of such structures for the particular case of the [[4-sphere]] remains open as of 2026. For any positive integer ''n'' other than 4, there are no exotic smooth structures <math>\R^n;</math> in other words, if ''n'' ≠ 4 then any smooth manifold homeomorphic to <math>\R^n</math> is diffeomorphic to <math>\R^n.</math><ref>Stallings (1962), in particular Corollary 5.2</ref>

== Construction ==

=== Construction from the failure of smooth surgery theory ===

Exotic <math>\R^4</math> arise from the failure of smooth [[surgery theory]], in particular glueing a disc <math>D^4</math> to its boundary sphere <math>S^3</math> not resulting in a smooth 4-manifold. Exotic 7-spheres called [[Milnor sphere]]s arise from a fully analogous failure of glueing a disc <math>D^8</math> to its boundary sphere <math>S^7</math> not resulting in a smooth 8-manifold. But the conclusions are different: In the latter case, <math>D^8\cong\mathbb{R}^8</math> has no exotic smooth structure, so <math>S^7</math> has to in order to explain the failure. In the former case, <math>S^3</math> has no exotic smooth structure due to [[Moise's theorem]],<ref>Scorpan 05, p. 101</ref> so <math>D^4\cong\mathbb{R}^4</math> has to in order to explain the failure.

==== Construction from the K3 surface ====

A concrete construction is the [[K3 surface]] <math>\mathrm{K3}</math>, described by the homogenous equation <math>x^4+y^4+z^4+w^4=0</math> in [[twistor space]] <math>\mathbb{C}P^3</math>.<ref>Freed & Uhlenbeck 84, p. 21</ref><ref>Scorpan 05, p. 130</ref> According to [[Freedman classification|Freedman's classification]],<ref name=":1">Freed & Uhlenbeck 84, p. 22-24</ref><ref name=":2">Scorpan 05, p. 240-243</ref> it is homeomorphic to the [[connected sum]] <math>2\overline{M_{E_8}}\#3(S^2\times S^2)</math> of twice the orientation-reversed [[E8 manifold]] <math>M_{E_8}</math> and thrice the [[complex surface]] <math>S^2\times S^2\cong\mathbb{C}P^1\times\mathbb{C}P^1</math> gained from the product of the [[Riemann sphere]] with itself. Although <math>\mathrm{K3}</math> is a smooth 4-manifold, <math>2\overline{M_{E_8}}\#k(S^2\times S^2)</math> isn't for <math>k=0,1,2</math>. For <math>k=0</math>, this follows from [[Donaldson's theorem]],<ref name=":1" /><ref>Scorpan 05, p. 243</ref> and for <math>k=1,2</math>, it was also shown by [[Simon Donaldson]],<ref>Scorpan 05, p. 248</ref> although Donaldson's theorem itself no longer applies. (A simpler argument was later obtained with [[Seiberg–Witten invariants]].) Hence a smooth surgery along the connecting sphere <math>S^3</math> to remove one, two or three <math>S^2\times S^2</math> from the smooth K3 surface <math>\mathrm{K3}</math> must fail.<ref>Freed & Uhlenbeck 84, p. 24-30</ref> (It is an open question whether this also holds for any connected sum of the K3 surface <math>\mathrm{K3}</math>, which is known as [[11/8 conjecture]].) In the simplest surgery of removing three <math>S^2\times S^2</math>, the failure spawns an exotic <math>\R^4</math> in <math>\#3(S^2\times S^2)</math>.

==== Construction from a nine-fold blow-up ====

The [[Intersection form of a 4-manifold|intersection form]] of the smooth [[complex surface]] <math>\mathbb{C}P^2\#9\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math>, the simplest example of an [[elliptic surface]] known as [[Dolgachev surface]], is <math>[+1]\oplus 9[-1]
\cong -E_8\oplus[+1]\oplus[-1]</math><ref name=":0" /> with the isomorphism coming from the [[Hasse–Minkowski theorem|Hesse–Minkowski theorem]]. It is therefore the same as for the topological 4-manifold <math>\overline{M_{E_8}}\#\mathbb{C}P^2\#*\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math> using the [[fake second complex projective space]], so Freedman's classification<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> claims both to be homeomorphic. In particular, that makes <math>\overline{M_{E_8}}\#\mathbb{C}P^2\#*\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math> smoothable. But a smooth surgery to remove <math>\mathbb{C}P^2</math> results in the non-smoothable manifold <math>\overline{M_{E_8}}\#*\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math>,<ref name=":2" /> which follows from its intersection form <math>-E_8\oplus[-1]</math> being negative definite and not diagonalizable, which Donaldson's theorem forbids if it was smoothable. The failure of this smooth surgery spawns an exotic <math>\R^4</math> in <math>\mathbb{C}P^2</math>.

==== Construction from a ten-fold blow-up ====

The previous construction can be expanded: The intersection form of the smooth complex surface <math>\mathbb{C}P^2\# 10\overline{\mathbb{C}P^9}</math> is <math>[+1]\oplus 10[-1]
\cong -E_8\oplus H\oplus[-1]</math>,<ref name=":0" /> the same as for the topological 4-manifold <math>\overline{M_{E_8}}\#(S^2\times S^2)\#*\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math>, so Freedman's classification<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> claims both to be homeomorphic and in particular the latter to be smoothable. But a smooth surgery to remove <math>S^2\times S^2</math> again results in the non-smoothable manifold <math>\overline{M_{E_8}}\#*\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}</math>. The failure of this smooth surgery spawns an exotic <math>\R^4</math> in <math>S^2\times S^2</math>.

=== Construction from the failure of the smooth h-cobordism theorem ===

According to Michael Freedman, the four-dimensional topological [[h-cobordism theorem]] holds, while according to Simon Donaldson, the four-dimensional smooth h-cobordism theorem doesn't hold. Let <math>W</math> be a smooth h-cobordism between smooth 4-manifolds <math>M</math> and <math>N</math>, for which there is no diffeomorphism <math>W\cong M\times[0,1]</math>, although there must be a homeomorphism <math>W\cong M\times[0,1]</math>. In this case there exists an open sub-cobordism <math>U\subset W</math> with a homeomorphism <math>U\cong D^4\times[0,1]\cong\mathbb{R}^4\times[0,1]</math> and a compact contractible sub-cobordism <math>K\subset U</math>, so that <math>W</math> and <math>U</math> are indeed smoothly trivial cobordisms outside of <math>K</math>, hence there are diffeomorphisms:
:<math>
W\setminus K
\cong(M\setminus K)\times[0,1];
</math>
:<math>
U\setminus K
\cong(U\cap M\setminus K)\times[0,1].
</math>
Now <math>U</math> connects the two open subsets <math>U\cap M\setminus K</math> and <math>U\cap N\setminus K</math>, which are homeomorphic to <math>\R^4</math>, but cannot diffeomorphic to <math>\R^4</math> as this would cause a diffeomorphism <math>W\cong M\times[0,1]</math>.<ref name=":0">Scorpan 05, p. 250-259</ref>

==Small exotic R<sup>4</sup>s==
An exotic <math>\R^4</math> is called '''small''' if it can be smoothly embedded as an open subset of the standard <math>\R^4.</math>

Small exotic <math>\R^4</math> can be constructed by starting with a non-trivial smooth 5-dimensional ''h''-[[cobordism]] (which exists by Donaldson's proof that the [[h-cobordism|''h''-cobordism theorem]] fails in this dimension) and using Freedman's theorem that the topological ''h''-cobordism theorem holds in this dimension.

==Large exotic R<sup>4</sup>s==
An exotic <math>\R^4</math> is called '''large''' if it cannot be smoothly embedded as an open subset of the standard <math>\R^4.</math>

Examples of large exotic <math>\R^4</math> can be constructed using the fact that compact 4-manifolds can often be split as a topological sum (by Freedman's work), but cannot be split as a smooth sum (by Donaldson's work).

{{harvs|txt| last1=Freedman | first1=Michael Hartley | last2=Taylor | first2=Laurence R. | title=A universal smoothing of four-space | url= http://projecteuclid.org/getRecord?id=euclid.jdg/1214440258 | mr=857376 | year=1986 | journal=Journal of Differential Geometry | issn=0022-040X | volume =24 | issue=1 | pages=69–78}} showed that there is a maximal exotic <math>\R^4,</math> into which all other <math>\R^4</math> can be smoothly embedded as open subsets.

==Related exotic structures==
[[Casson handle]]s are homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb{D}^2 \times \R^2</math> by Freedman's theorem (where <math>\mathbb{D}^2</math> is the closed unit disc) but it follows from Donaldson's theorem that they are not all diffeomorphic to <math>\mathbb{D}^2 \times \R^2.</math> In other words, some Casson handles are exotic <math>\mathbb{D}^2 \times \R^2.</math>

It is not known (as of 2024) whether or not there are any exotic 4-spheres; such an exotic 4-sphere would be a counterexample to the smooth [[generalized Poincaré conjecture]] in dimension 4. Some plausible candidates are given by [[Exotic sphere#4-dimensional exotic spheres and Gluck twists|Gluck twists]].
